lead: This unit explains how electrons are arranged in atoms, molecules and solids, and how that arrangement controls colour, magnetism and stability. After it you can use wavefunctions and MO diagrams, count electrons in complexes, apply crystal field theory, and predict hard-soft preferences.
about: This unit starts with the quantum picture of electrons: wave-particle duality, uncertainty, the Schrödinger equation and effective nuclear charge. These ideas explain atomic orbitals and periodic trends. Chapter 1.4 uses molecular orbital theory to build bonding in diatomics, butadiene and benzene. Chapter 1.5 extends bonding to solids: ionic, covalent, metallic and hydrogen. The next three chapters move to coordination compounds: electron counting with EAN and the 18-electron rule, crystal field splitting of d orbitals, and the colour and magnetic behaviour that follow. Chapter 1.9 classifies acids and bases as hard or soft, connecting stability and reactivity. Worked examples use O2, NaCl, Ni(CO)4, Cr3+ complexes and AgI.

chapters.idea: Light and matter show both wave and particle behaviour, and the uncertainty principle limits how precisely position and momentum can be known together.
chapters.depth: Black-body radiation, Planck's hypothesis, photoelectric effect, de Broglie wavelength and electron diffraction. State Heisenberg's relation Δx Δp ≥ ħ/2 and apply it to an electron. Only a few universities teach this in first semester; keep the algebra to one dimension.

figure.aria: A hyperbola shows the smallest allowed momentum spread falling as position spread grows; points above the curve are allowed.

chapters.example: A photon has wavelength 400 nm. Find its momentum and the minimum position uncertainty if its momentum is known to 0.1%. Use p = h/λ = 1.66 × 10⁻²⁷ kg m s⁻¹; Δp = 1.66 × 10⁻³⁰ kg m s⁻¹; then Δx ≥ ħ/(2Δp) = 3.2 × 10⁻⁵ m, about 0.032 mm.
chapters.trap: Do not treat Δx as the size of the particle; it is the standard deviation of many repeated position measurements.
chapters.prereq: School physics: waves, photons and kinetic energy.
chapters.leave: Hydrogen energy levels and orbital shapes go to 1.2; spectroscopy selection rules go to Unit 2.

chapters.idea: The Schrödinger equation gives allowed wavefunctions and quantised energies, first for a particle in a box and then for the hydrogen atom.
chapters.depth: Postulates of quantum mechanics, Born interpretation of ψ, time-independent Schrödinger equation. Solve the 1D box: ψ_n and E_n. Give radial and angular parts of H-atom wavefunctions and the meaning of n, l, m. Only a few universities teach this in Unit 1; do not derive the hydrogen solution in full.

figure.aria: A rising curve shows box energy levels increasing as n squared, with n on the horizontal axis.

chapters.example: Find the ground-state energy of an electron in a 1D box of length 1.00 nm. E₁ = h²/(8mL²) = 6.02 × 10⁻²⁰ J = 0.376 eV.
chapters.trap: The box energy depends on L²; doubling the box length lowers E by a factor of four, not two.
chapters.leave: Multielectron atoms go to 1.3; molecular orbitals go to 1.4; spectroscopic transitions go to Unit 2.

chapters.idea: Inner electrons screen the nuclear charge, so the outer electron feels an effective nuclear charge Zeff that sets size, ionisation energy and electronegativity trends.
chapters.depth: Define Z, S and Zeff = Z − S. Use Slater's rules for ns and np electrons. Relate Zeff to atomic radius, ionisation energy, electron affinity and electronegativity across a period and down a group. Only a few universities teach this; keep examples to main-group atoms.

figure.aria: A flow diagram shows nuclear charge and screening combining into Zeff, which sets atomic radius and ionization energy.

chapters.example: Find Zeff for the 3s electron of sodium (Z = 11). Configuration 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s¹. S = 8 × 0.85 + 2 × 1.00 = 8.80; Zeff = 11 − 8.80 = 2.20.
chapters.trap: Slater's 0.35 same-shell count applies to ns/np electrons; nd/nf electrons use different screening rules.
chapters.leave: Detailed periodic anomalies go to inorganic courses; X-ray screening in atoms is not needed here.

chapters.idea: Molecular orbital theory combines atomic orbitals into bonding and antibonding MOs; filling them gives bond order, magnetism and π-electron patterns.
chapters.depth: Build MO diagrams for H2, He2, N2, O2 and F2. Define σ, π, σ*, π*, HOMO, LUMO and bond order. Draw π MOs of butadiene (four p orbitals, four π electrons) and benzene (six p orbitals, six π electrons, degenerate e1g set). Some syllabi call this orbital theory; keep group theory out.

figure.aria: A left-to-right flow shows atomic orbitals combining into molecular orbitals, then electrons filling them and bond order being counted.

chapters.example: Use MO theory to find the bond order and unpaired electrons of O2. Configuration σ2s² σ*2s² σ2p² π2p⁴ π*2p². Bond order = (8 − 4)/2 = 2; two unpaired electrons in π* give paramagnetism.
chapters.trap: O2 has a double bond but is paramagnetic; a simple Lewis structure with all electrons paired misses this.
chapters.leave: Band structure of semiconductors goes to Unit 6; aromatic substitution mechanisms go to organic chemistry.

chapters.idea: Solids are held together by ionic, covalent, metallic or hydrogen bonding, and the bonding type explains melting point, conductivity and solubility.
chapters.depth: Compare ionic (NaCl), covalent network (diamond), metallic (Fe) and hydrogen-bonded (ice) solids. Use radius ratio r+/r− to predict coordination number 4, 6 or 8. Mention van der Waals solids. Some syllabi add spinel, perovskite, quasicrystals and amorphous solids; treat these as structure types in one line.

figure.aria: A tree groups solids into ionic, covalent, metallic and hydrogen-bonded types with one example each.

chapters.example: Predict the coordination number of Na+ in NaCl from r(Na+) = 102 pm and r(Cl−) = 181 pm. Ratio = 102/181 = 0.564. This lies between 0.414 and 0.732, so Na+ is six-coordinate (octahedral).
chapters.trap: Radius ratio gives a prediction; real structures also depend on charge balance and lattice energy, so do not treat the ranges as exact.
chapters.leave: Band theory and semiconductors go to Unit 6; defects and crystal growth go to materials courses.

chapters.idea: Coordination compounds obey electron-counting rules: EAN counts electrons around the metal, and the 18-electron rule counts valence electrons for organometallic stability.
chapters.depth: Define ligand, coordination number, oxidation state, EAN and 18-electron rule. Count CO, halides, phosphines and η-ligands as donors. Apply to [Fe(CN)6]4−, [Ni(CO)4] and ferrocene. Some syllabi call this the effective atomic number rule; keep to main examples.

figure.aria: A flow diagram adds metal d electrons and ligand electrons to a total, then checks it against 18.

chapters.example: Count electrons in [Ni(CO)4] and test the 18-electron rule. Ni is oxidation state 0, so d10 = 10 electrons; four CO ligands donate 4 × 2 = 8; total = 18.
chapters.trap: CO is a neutral two-electron donor; do not count it as CO2+ or add charge to the metal.
chapters.prereq: 1.3 for electron configuration; 1.4 for MO ideas.
chapters.leave: Crystal field splitting goes to 1.7; catalytic cycles go to Unit 5 and 1.9.

chapters.idea: Ligands split the five d orbitals into sets of different energy; the size and pattern of splitting depend on geometry and ligand field strength.
chapters.depth: Crystal field theory for octahedral, tetrahedral and square-planar complexes. Label eg and t2g in octahedral; e and t2 in tetrahedral. Define Δo, Δt = 4/9 Δo and CFSE. Distinguish high-spin and low-spin d4 to d7. Some syllabi call this ligand field theory; keep the electrostatic model.

figure.aria: A tree splits d orbitals under octahedral, tetrahedral and square-planar fields into lower and upper energy sets.

chapters.example: Find the CFSE of [Cr(H2O)6]3+. Cr is +3, d3, octahedral. Configuration t2g³. CFSE = 3 × (−0.4Δo) = −1.2Δo; no pairing energy is needed.
chapters.trap: Tetrahedral splitting Δt is much smaller than octahedral Δo; most tetrahedral complexes are high spin.
chapters.prereq: 1.6 for complex formation and oxidation states.
chapters.leave: Colour and magnetic moments go to 1.8; MO description of bonding in complexes is not needed.

chapters.idea: d–d transitions absorb visible light and give colour, while unpaired d electrons give paramagnetism; both follow from crystal field splitting.
chapters.depth: Explain colour as absorption of a wavelength and transmission of the complementary colour. Use Δo = hc/λ. Use spin-only formula μ = √(n(n+2)) BM. Compare high-spin and low-spin Fe3+ complexes. Only a few universities teach this depth; keep to one metal centre.

figure.aria: A plot of absorbance against wavelength has a strong peak near 500 nanometres, the light absorbed by a d–d transition.

chapters.example: For [Fe(CN)6]3−, Fe is +3, d5, low spin with one unpaired electron. Find μ. μ = √(1 × 3) = 1.73 BM.
chapters.trap: The spin-only formula fails when orbital angular momentum contributes, especially for Co2+ and some tetrahedral complexes.
chapters.leave: UV-visible and NMR spectra go to Unit 2; magnetic materials go to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: Hard acids and bases are small, highly charged and unpolarisable; soft acids and bases are large and polarisable; hard pairs with hard and soft with soft.
chapters.depth: Define hardness and softness using charge density and polarisability. Classify common cations and anions. Use HSAB to predict stability of AgI versus AgF, and to explain chelation and catalysis. Only a few universities teach this; avoid quantitative scales.

figure.aria: A two-set Venn diagram places hard and soft acids and bases apart, with borderline cases in the overlap.

chapters.example: AgI or AgF: which is more stable by HSAB? Ag+ is soft and I− is soft, so AgI is favoured. F− is hard and pairs poorly with soft Ag+, so AgF is less favoured.
chapters.trap: Hardness is not the same as acid strength; a strong acid can be soft or hard, so do not use pH to classify.
chapters.prereq: 1.5 for ionic bonding; 1.6 for metal ions.
chapters.leave: Buffer pH calculations go to water chemistry; catalytic mechanisms go to Unit 5.

links: wavefunctions give electron density and screening
MO and hybrid orbitals explain solid bonding
ionic and covalent ideas lead to ligand fields
electron count and geometry set up CFT
